translations.title: Rima XL: Su mano entre mis manos
translations.text:
Her hand in my hands,
her eyes in my eyes,
her loving head
resting on my shoulder.
God knows how many times,
with leisurely steps,
we have wandered together
beneath the tall elms
that lend her house
mystery and shade at the entrance!
And yesterday… scarcely a year
has passed, as swift as a breath;
with what exquisite grace,
with what admirable poise,
she said to me, as an officious friend
introduced us:
“I think I’ve seen you somewhere.” “Ah!” fools,
you drawing-room gossips
of polished manners,
who go about hunting
for amorous intrigues:
What a story you have missed!
What a delicious morsel
to devour
in whispers, in a circle,
behind a fan
of feathers and gold!

Discreet and chaste moon,
leafy, lofty elms,
walls of her house,
threshold of her doorway,
be silent, and let the secret
never leave you!
Be silent; as for my part,
I have forgotten everything:
and she… she… no mask
could resemble her face!

translations.title: Rima LXXXIX: Si copia tu frente
translations.text:
If the nearby river’s pure current
is mirrored on your brow,
and you see your face glowing with love,
it is I, hiding
at the bottom of the water,
who, mad with love, invite you to love;
it is I, who, having sought a home in your breast,
send my ardent gaze into your eyes,
my divine flame…
and the fire I feel lights your face.

If, in the middle of the valley,
your lively love turns to weariness,
your step falters, your body bends…
it is I, beloved master,
who, in unseen bonds
of yearning love, clasp you in my arms;
it is I who weave the flowered carpet
that restores the strength of life to your body;
it is I who follow you,
dreaming of you on the wings of the wind.

If, as you lie in bed,
you happen to hear a heavenly harmony
that fills your innocent heart with joy,
it is I, my life…;
it is I who raise
my fervent song to the tranquil sky;
it is I who, lightly crossing the air
by an unknown, shifting path,
eager for peace,
thirsting for love, enter your soul.

translations.title: Rima IV: No digáis que agotado su tesoro
Rima XXVII: Despierta, tiemblo al mirarte
translations.text:
Awake, I tremble as I gaze at you;
asleep, I dare to look at you;
therefore, soul of my soul,
I keep watch while you sleep.

Awake, you laugh, and as you laugh, your restless lips
seem to me like scarlet lightning
snaking across
a sky of snow.

Asleep, the corners of your mouth
fold into a faint smile,
soft as the luminous trail
left by a dying sun.
Sleep!

Awake, you look, and as you look, your eyes,
moist, gleam
like the blue wave on whose crest
the flashing sun strikes.

Asleep, through your eyelids,
you pour a tranquil radiance,
as a tempered beam of light spills
from a crystal lamp…
Sleep!

Awake, you speak, and as you speak, your vibrant
words seem like
a rain of pearls pouring in torrents
into a golden cup.

Asleep, in the murmur of your breath,
measured and soft,
I hear a poem that my loving soul
understands…
Sleep!

I have laid my hand upon my heart
so its beat will not sound
and disturb the solemn calm
of the night.

I have already closed the shutters
of your balcony, so the vexing dawn
will not enter
and wake you…
Sleep!

translations.title: Rima LXX: Cuántas veces al pie de las musgosas
translations.text:
How many times, at the foot of the moss-covered
walls that shelter it,
I heard the little bell that, at midnight,
calls to matins!

How many times the silver moon traced
my sad shadow
beside the cypress that peers over
the walls of its garden!

When the church was wrapped in shadow
beneath its pierced Gothic arch,
how many times I saw the lamp’s glow
tremble on the panes!

Though the wind whistled
in the tower’s dark corners,
amid the choir’s voices I could hear
her voice, clear and vibrant.

On winter nights, if some frightened passerby
dared cross the deserted square,
seeing me, he would
hurry his step.

And once an old woman at the spinning wheel
said in the morning
that perhaps I was the soul
of some sacristan who died in sin.

In the dark I knew every corner
of the churchyard and entrance;
the nettles growing there may still keep
the marks of my feet.

The owls, who followed me in fright
with their eyes of flame,
in time came to look at me
as a good companion.

Beside me, unafraid, the reptiles
crawled along;
I even saw the mute granite saints
greet me!

translations.title: Rima LXXXIV: Yo soy el rayo, la dulce brisa
translations.text:
I am the lightning, the gentle breeze,
the burning tear, the fresh smile,
the wandering flower, the broken branch;
I am the one who quivers, a sharpened arrow.

In my essence there are, as in flowers,
soft vapors of a thousand perfumes,
and their fascinating fragrance
bewilders the soul of whoever adores.
I lavish my aromas everywhere
and soothe the most dreadful pain;
in sweet, tender, pleasing delirium
I change the harshest, cruelest torment.
Ah, I bind hearts in chains,
but their links are made of flowers.
I sail across the seas,
I travel on the wind,
I drive sorrows
from the mind.
I, in joy or grief,
divide my gifts among mortals
with serene face.
Terrible power, which at my whim
brings smiles or anger;
power that sets a frozen soul ablaze
when I angrily loose my sharpened arrow.

I give sweet smiles to beautiful women;
I tint their snowy cheeks with roses;
I moisten their lips, and make their glances
promise joys beyond imagining.
I make repose kind, pleasing, alluring,
or banish sweet sleep from living beings.

Everything pays homage to my might;
all are vassals to my crown.
I am Love, king of the world, tyrant girl;
love me, and tomorrow
you shall be queen.

translations.title: Rima XCIV: Patriarcas que fuisteis la semilla
translations.text:
Patriarchs, who were the seed
of the tree of faith in distant centuries,
pray for us to the divine conqueror of death.

Prophets, who in your inspiration tore
asunder the mysterious veil of the future,
pray for us to him who brought light from darkness.

Innocent souls, Holy Innocents,
who swell the angels’ choir,
pray for us to him who called the children to his side.

Apostles, who laid in the world
the Church’s mighty foundation,
pray for us to him who is the keeper of truth.

Martyrs, who won your palm
in the circus arena, red with blood,
pray for us to him who gave you strength in battle.

Virgins like lilies,
whom summer clothed in snow and gold,
pray for us to him who is the source of life and beauty.

Monks, who in life’s struggle
sought peace in the silent cloister,
pray for us to him who is the rainbow of calm amid storms.

Doctors, whose pens bequeathed us
a rich treasure of virtue and learning,
pray for us to him who is an inexhaustible stream of knowledge.

Soldiers in Christ’s army,
all holy women and men,
pray that he may forgive our sins,
he who lives and reigns among you.

translations.title: Rima LXXVI: En la imponente nave
translations.text:
In the imposing nave
of the Byzantine church,
I saw a Gothic tomb in the uncertain
light that trembled on the painted [windows].

Her hands upon her breast,
and in her hands a book,
a beautiful woman rested
upon the urn, a marvel of the sculptor’s art.

Beneath the gentle weight
of the abandoned body,
as if it were soft feather and satin,
her granite bed seemed to fold.

The divine radiance
of her last smile
still guarded her face, as the sky keeps
the fleeting ray of the dying sun.

At the stone pillow,
seated on its edge,
two angels, a finger to their lips,
enforced silence in the chamber.

She did not seem dead;
under the massive arches
she seemed to sleep in the half-light,
and in dreams to behold paradise.

I approached the nave’s
shadowy corner,
like one who comes with silent steps
to the cradle where a child sleeps.

I gazed at her a moment,
and that warm radiance,
that stone bed offering, beside the wall,
another empty place nearby,

stirred in my soul
a thirst for the infinite,
a longing for that life in death,
for which centuries are but an instant…

Weary from the struggle
in which I live and fight,
sometimes I remember with envy
that dark, hidden corner.

I remember that silent,
pale woman and say:
Oh, how quiet is death’s love!
How peaceful the sleep of the tomb!

translations.title: Rima XII: Porque son, niña, tus ojos
translations.text:
Because your eyes, my girl,
are green as the sea, you complain:
the naiads’ eyes are green,
Minerva’s were green,
and green are the pupils
of the prophet’s houris.

Green is the forest’s finery
and ornament in spring.
Among its seven colors
the rainbow displays it bright.
Emeralds are green,
green is the color of hope,
as are the ocean’s waves
and the poets’ laurel.

Your tender cheek is
a rose covered with frost,
where the petals’ crimson
shows through the pearls.
And yet
I know you complain
because you think
your eyes make it less fair;
but do not think so:
your pupils seem,
moist, green, and restless,
like young almond leaves
trembling in the breeze.

Your ruby mouth is
a purple pomegranate split open,
inviting us in summer
to quench our thirst there.
And yet
I know you complain
because you think
your eyes make it less fair;
but do not think so:
when your pupils flash in anger,
they seem like sea waves
breaking against the Cantabrian cliffs.

Your brow, crowned
with gold curled in a broad braid,
is a snowy peak on which the day
reflects its last light.
And yet
I know you complain
because you think
your eyes make it less fair;
but that is not so:
among your golden lashes,
beside your temples, they resemble
brooches of emerald and gold
fastened in white ermine.

translations.title: Soneto
translations.text:
To see whether her eyes were like those
whose fame had spread among the shepherds,
Dórida one day gazed at them in a spring
and, seeing them so, spoke thus:

translations.title: Amor, mueve las alas tan alto...
translations.text:
Love, who moves your wings so high…

Sonnet
To see whether her eyes were like those
whose fame had spread among the shepherds,
Dórida one day gazed at them in a spring
and, seeing them so, spoke thus:

translations.title: Madrigal
translations.text:
Clear, serene eyes,
if you are praised for a sweet glance,
why, when you look at me, do you look in anger?
If, when most compassionate,
you seem most beautiful to the one who looks at you,
do not look at me with ire,
or you will seem less lovely.
Ah, torment, fierce and wild!
Clear, serene eyes,
since this is how you look at me, at least look at me.

translations.title: Cubrir los bellos ojos
translations.text:
To cover your lovely eyes
with the hand that has already slain me
was surely a stratagem;
you thought thereby to double my distress.

But the good from that stratagem
has far outweighed the harm,
for the sun’s strange radiance
can be seen even while concealed.

So, though you meant to hide
your beauty, unique and immense,
I forgive you the offense,
since veiled, you let me see them better.

translations.title: Al monte donde fue Cartago
Ponzoña que se bebe por los ojos
translations.text:
Poison drunk through the eyes,
a harsh prison, sweet to thought,
a cruel golden snare, a sweet torment,
confusion of madness and desire;

beautiful flowers mingled with thorns,
food that leaves the heart hungry,
a harm that always escapes correction,
a mine of pleasure filled with grief;

uncertain, deceptive hopes,
a treasure seen between dreams,
a good that holds within it nothing but shadow;

useless, hard-won riches,
a harbor never found, though it seems near:
these are the effects of what is called Love.

translations.title: Qué aprovecha, señor, andar buscando
translations.text:
What good, my lord, is it to go hunting
now for the fierce, bristly wild boar?
What good to pursue the swift deer,
or shoot with cruel arrows dipped in poison?

What good, my lord, to flush the heron
with a falcon soaring high?
What good to shoot so true,
killing a hare here, a pheasant there?

if your thoughts always follow you,
if you carry them in your soul,
if you are bound to them when most at liberty,

if you bear your thoughts so tenderly
that where you are most free and content,
you go after the quarry with them entangled.

translations.title: Entre armas, guerra, fuego, ira y furores
translations.text:
Amid arms, war, fire, anger, and fury,
which hold the haughty Frenchman captive,
when the air is darkest and thickest,
there the fierce ardor of love grips me.

I look at the sky, the trees, the flowers,
and in them I find my pain expressed;
in the coldest and most bitter season
my fears are born and green again.

I say through tears: “Oh, sweet spring,
when will I see my hope
bring some peace to my soul?”

But I fear my cruel fate means my end
must lie so far from my beloved
amid war and fury, anger, arms, and fire.

translations.title: Al príncipe de Ascoli
translations.text:
Shepherd, what occasion, what strange thing,
what cruel misfortune, what fierce fate
brought you to tend a new flock
so far from your beloved, here on this mountain?

The strange novelty of this deed
has left me confused and unsettled,
knowing you are not free of the cares
you used to bear back in Spain.

Take care as you travel through this land;
if you have your freedom, guard it well,
for the nymphs here are wary.

For such beauty, shepherd, you may lose it,
for she will give you a thousand loving signs,
then wage barbarous war upon you.
